lesson.title: Reading the Bar Code: Turning a PES Spectrum into an Electron Configuration
lesson.summary: A photoelectron spectrum plots binding energy against the relative number of electrons at each energy, and learning to read peak positions and heights lets chemists reconstruct an atom's full electron configuration from data alone.
lesson.body:
A photoelectron spectrum is a graph, and like any graph, it only gives up its meaning once you know how to read the axes. By convention, the horizontal axis shows binding energy, usually plotted decreasing from left to right, so tightly held core electrons with huge binding energies appear on the far left and loosely held valence electrons appear on the far right. The vertical axis shows relative number of electrons, essentially how many photoelectrons were detected at each binding energy. Each distinct peak on the graph corresponds to one subshell of electrons in the atom, exactly as introduced in the photoelectron spectroscopy chapter.

Two pieces of information hide inside every peak, and both matter. The peak's position along the binding energy axis tells you how tightly that subshell of electrons is held, with subshells closer to the nucleus producing peaks far to the left at high binding energy, and outer valence subshells producing peaks close to the right at low binding energy. The peak's height, its relative intensity, tells you how many electrons occupy that subshell, because more electrons in a given subshell means more photoelectrons get ejected at that particular binding energy, producing a taller signal. Reading a PES spectrum is therefore a matter of counting peaks for the number of distinct subshells, noting their left-to-right order for relative binding energy, and comparing their heights for relative electron population.

Neon's spectrum, from the previous chapter, makes an ideal worked example. It shows three peaks: one far to the left at a binding energy near 84.0 MJ/mol, one in the middle near 4.68 MJ/mol, and one closer to the right near 2.08 MJ/mol. The relative heights of those three peaks come out in a ratio of 2 to 2 to 6. Reading that directly as electron counts gives 2 electrons in the first, innermost subshell, 2 in the second, and 6 in the third, which is exactly the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6. Add those populations up, 2 + 2 + 6 = 10, and you recover neon's atomic number without ever being told it in advance, straight from the graph.

Larger atoms produce more complex spectra, but the same reading strategy scales up cleanly. Peaks cluster into groups separated by large gaps in binding energy, one cluster per principal energy level, or shell, with smaller gaps separating the individual subshells within a cluster, an s subshell peak sitting at somewhat higher binding energy than a p subshell peak from the same shell, since s electrons on average sit slightly closer to the nucleus. Within each cluster, the relative peak heights still track electron counts directly, so a chemist can reconstruct an entire electron configuration, shell by shell and subshell by subshell, purely from where the peaks fall and how tall they stand.

This turns PES from a neat physics demonstration into a genuine analytical tool. An unexpected peak height, say a 2p peak only two thirds as tall as expected, signals that electrons are missing relative to a neutral atom, which is exactly what you would see from a cation that has lost valence electrons. An unfamiliar pattern of peaks, matched against known binding energies, can even help identify an unknown element. In every case, the underlying logic is the same graph-reading skill: position tells you binding energy, height tells you electron count, and together they tell you exactly how an atom's electrons are arranged.
